title: Unit 2: Computational Thinking, Data Structures & Algorithms

questions.question: Which pillar of computational thinking involves breaking down a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems?
questions.explanation: Decomposition divides a complex problem into modular, independently solvable components.

questions.question: Which computational thinking technique filters out irrelevant details to focus exclusively on essential characteristics?
questions.explanation: Abstraction removes extraneous real-world complexities, allowing the modeler to focus on core logic and properties.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of $n$ elements?
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the search interval in every step, resulting in a logarithmic runtime complexity of $O(\log n)$.

questions.question: Which prerequisite MUST be satisfied before binary search can be executed on a dataset?

options.B: The dataset must contain only prime integers
options.C: The data elements must be stored in a circular linked list
options.D: The array size must be an exact power of two

questions.explanation: Binary search relies on order comparisons to divide intervals; unsorted datasets will produce incorrect results.

questions.question: Which data structure operates on a strict Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) protocol?
questions.explanation: A stack inserts and removes elements from the same end (top), adhering to LIFO behavior (e.g., function call stacks, undo buffers).

questions.question: What will happen if a program executes a `pop()` operation on an empty stack?
questions.explanation: Attempting to retrieve or delete an element from a stack that contains no data results in a Stack Underflow condition.

questions.question: Which data structure operates on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle, where insertions happen at the rear and deletions at the front?
questions.explanation: Queues process items in arrival order (FIFO), widely used in CPU scheduling, print spooling, and breadth-first search.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of a Singly Linked List over a static Array of fixed size?

options.A: Dynamic size allocation without requiring contiguous memory blocks
options.B: Constant-time $O(1)$ random access to any element by index
options.C: Zero memory overhead for pointer references

questions.explanation: Linked lists allocate nodes dynamically in fragmented memory, easily expanding without costly array resizing or reallocations.

questions.question: In a Doubly Linked List, what do the two pointers stored inside each node point to?

options.A: The next node and the previous node
options.B: The root node and the leaf node
options.C: The array base address and stack pointer
options.D: The left child and right child in a heap

questions.explanation: Each node in a doubly linked list contains data, a forward pointer (`next`), and a backward pointer (`prev`), allowing bidirectional traversal.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Bubble Sort on an array of $n$ elements in descending order?
questions.explanation: Bubble sort compares and swaps adjacent pairs across $n-1$ passes, performing $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons, yielding $O(n^2)$.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm employs a Divide-and-Conquer paradigm with guaranteed $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time complexity?
questions.explanation: Merge sort divides the list into halves recursively and merges them back in sorted order with consistent $O(n \log n)$ efficiency.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quicksort when an unbalanced pivot (e.g., smallest element) is consistently selected?
questions.explanation: When Quicksort partitions the array into $0$ and $n-1$ elements in every step (degenerate tree), its time complexity degrades to $O(n^2)$.

questions.question: In a Binary Search Tree (BST), what property must hold for all keys in the left subtree of any given node $X$?

options.A: All keys must be strictly less than the key of node $X$
options.B: All keys must be strictly greater than the key of node $X$
options.C: All keys must be equal to the hash code of node $X$
options.D: All keys must be exact powers of 2

questions.explanation: By definition of a BST, every key in a node's left subtree is smaller, and every key in its right subtree is greater than the node's key.

questions.question: Which tree traversal algorithm visits nodes in the exact order: Left Subtree $\rightarrow$ Root $\rightarrow$ Right Subtree?
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits left-root-right. When executed on a Binary Search Tree, it outputs all values in ascending sorted order.

questions.question: Which asymptotic notation represents the tight mathematical upper bound on the growth rate of an algorithm's execution time?
questions.explanation: Big-O notation specifies an asymptotic upper bound, representing the maximum time or space an algorithm will consume for large inputs.

questions.question: Which graph traversal technique explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, utilizing a Stack (or recursion)?
questions.explanation: DFS traverses vertex paths to their terminal depth before backtracking, naturally implemented with a stack data structure.

questions.question: Which graph traversal technique explores all neighboring vertices at the present depth level before moving deeper, utilizing a Queue?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level using a FIFO queue, guaranteeing the shortest path in unweighted graphs.

questions.question: How is a graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges represented using an Adjacency Matrix?

options.A: A 2D array of size $V \times V$ where entry $[i][j]$ indicates whether an edge connects vertex $i$ to vertex $j$
options.B: A 1D linked list containing only leaf nodes
options.C: A hash table storing edge weights indexed by prime modulo numbers
options.D: A binary heap storing node degrees in descending order

questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix is a $V \times V$ matrix where cells contain 1 (or edge weight) if an edge exists, and 0 if no edge connects the vertices.

questions.question: For a sparse graph with few edges ($E \ll V^2$), which data structure is far more space-efficient than an adjacency matrix?
questions.explanation: An adjacency list stores an array/list of edges for each vertex, consuming only $O(V + E)$ memory compared to $O(V^2)$ for a matrix.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of looking up a value in an ideal Hash Table with zero collisions?
questions.explanation: A hash function computes direct array bucket indices, yielding constant-time $O(1)$ retrieval in the average/ideal case.

questions.question: In hash table collision resolution, what does 'Separate Chaining' involve?

options.A: Attaching a linked list to each hash bucket to hold multiple colliding keys
options.B: Probing consecutively through the array until the next open slot is found
options.C: Rehashing the table using a cryptographically secure SHA-256 algorithm
options.D: Deleting the previously stored value to overwrite the bucket

questions.explanation: Separate chaining resolves hash collisions by maintaining a linked list of all key-value entries that hash to the same bucket index.

questions.question: What is a recursive function in computer algorithms?

options.A: A function that solves a problem by calling itself with smaller sub-problems until a base case is reached
options.B: A function that executes an infinite while-loop without CPU interrupts
options.C: A method that can only be invoked from an external operating system shell
options.D: A subroutine that converts high-level Python code into machine language

questions.explanation: Recursion occurs when a function invokes itself directly or indirectly, terminating when reaching defined base cases.

questions.question: What happens if a recursive function does not include a properly reachable base case?

options.A: Infinite recursion occurs, leading to a Call Stack Overflow crash
options.B: The algorithm executes in instantaneous $O(1)$ time
options.C: The compiler automatically rewrites the code into bubble sort
options.D: The computer reboots into safe mode

questions.explanation: Without a base case, recursion continues allocating stack frames indefinitely until the system runs out of call stack memory.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height $h$ (where root height = 0)?
questions.explanation: The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height $h$ is given by the geometric series $\sum_{i=0}^h 2^i = 2^{h+1} - 1$.

questions.question: Which algorithmic design approach builds up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most immediate, local benefit?
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step hoping it leads to a globally optimal solution (e.g., Dijkstra's, Kruskal's).

questions.question: Which algorithm design technique solves sub-problems once and stores their results in a lookup table (memoization) to avoid redundant recalculation?
questions.explanation: Dynamic Programming optimizes recursive problems with overlapping subproblems by caching computed answers (memoization or tabulation).

questions.question: What is the Big-O space complexity of storing an array of $n$ integer elements?
questions.explanation: An array of $n$ elements requires storage directly proportional to $n$, resulting in linear $O(n)$ space complexity.

questions.question: In an undirected graph with $V$ vertices and no self-loops, what is the maximum number of edges it can contain?
questions.explanation: In an undirected simple complete graph, each vertex connects to every other vertex, yielding $\binom{V}{2} = \frac{V(V-1)}{2}$ edges.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is recognized as being 'in-place' with $O(1)$ auxiliary memory requirement?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort operates directly within the input array by shifting elements, needing only $O(1)$ extra space.

questions.question: Which linear data structure allows insertion and deletion operations from BOTH ends (front and rear)?
questions.explanation: A deque (double-ended queue) is a generalized queue supporting insertion and deletion at both the front and back.

questions.question: In a Max-Heap binary tree, what relationship must hold between any parent node $P$ and its children $C$?

options.A: The key of parent $P$ is always greater than or equal to the keys of its children $C$
options.B: The key of parent $P$ is strictly smaller than the left child
options.C: The root must always have a value equal to zero
options.D: The left child must always be prime and the right child composite

questions.explanation: In a max-heap, the max-heap property requires every parent node to have a key greater than or equal to its child nodes, with the maximum at the root.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of deleting the minimum element in an optimal binary Min-Heap of $n$ elements?
questions.explanation: Extracting the root takes $O(1)$, but restoring heap order via sift-down / heapify requires traversing the tree height: $O(\log n)$.

questions.question: What is the primary characteristic of an algorithm described as 'Stable' in sorting theory?

options.A: It preserves the relative input order of records with equal keys
options.B: It never triggers hardware memory page faults
options.C: It runs in identical clock cycles regardless of CPU architecture

questions.explanation: A stable sorting algorithm guarantees that items with identical keys maintain their original relative positional order after sorting.

questions.question: What does the expression $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$ characterize in the Master Theorem?

options.A: Merge Sort runtime complexity, solving to $\Theta(n \log n)$
options.B: Binary search runtime, solving to $\Theta(\log n)$

questions.explanation: This standard recurrence splits the problem into two halves with linear merge cost, yielding $\Theta(n \log n)$ by Case 2 of the Master Theorem.

questions.question: Which data structure is universally utilized by operating systems to handle recursive function calls and local variable allocation?
questions.explanation: The call stack tracks active subroutines, pushing stack frames (parameters, return address, local variables) on invocation and popping on return.
